summary: Jesus sends the Twelve to proclaim and heal with deliberate dependence, while Herod wonders who Jesus is. After feeding a multitude, Jesus asks the same identity question: Peter names God's Messiah, but Jesus immediately says the Son of Man must suffer and calls everyone to cross-shaped following. On the mountain, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about the ‘exodus’ he will fulfill at Jerusalem; the divine voice commands listening. Below, disciples cannot free a boy, misunderstand a second passion warning, compete for greatness, police an outsider, and want fire on a Samaritan village. At 9:51 Jesus resolutely sets his face toward Jerusalem, and three would-be followers hear the journey's cost.
whyItMatters: Confessing the right title is not enough if Messiah is still imagined as domination. Luke turns the book at the moment glory, suffering, Scripture, failed discipleship, rejected hospitality, and determined journey converge. The road to Jerusalem will teach what following this king means.

context.author: Luke arranging identity traditions around the major 9:51 travel hinge
context.audience: Disciples tempted by power, status, exclusion, and avoidance of the cross
context.setting: Galilean villages, a deserted feeding place, prayer, a mountain, a crowd below, Samaritan territory, and the road south
context.literaryForm: Mission, royal question, feeding, confession, passion prediction, epiphany, exorcism, correction scenes, and journey call sayings

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.”
keyVerses.why: The title is correct, but the following verses redefine its path through suffering and service.

keyVerses.text: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
keyVerses.why: Discipleship follows the Messiah's self-giving route rather than using him to secure the self.

keyVerses.text: It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem
keyVerses.why: A biblical idiom of resolve opens the long travel narrative and aims beyond death toward being ‘taken up.’

questions.question: Why send the Twelve without provisions?
questions.answer: The instructions make them dependent on hospitality and keep mission from looking like extraction or self-protection. They bring proclamation and healing, remain with hosts rather than trading upward, and leave resistant places without coercion. Luke does not turn this specific mission into a universal ban on planning.

questions.question: Why is Herod's question repeated by Jesus?
questions.answer: Herod hears competing rumors and wants to see Jesus; later Jesus asks what crowds and disciples say. The repetition moves identity from curiosity toward confession. Herod's desire will finally produce spectacle-seeking in chapter 23, while disciples must learn that correct words require a transformed expectation.

questions.question: What does the feeding reveal beyond miraculous quantity?
questions.answer: Jesus tells the disciples to give food, organizes the crowd, blesses and breaks bread, and leaves abundant fragments. The scene evokes wilderness provision and anticipates table language without being reducible to Eucharist. Need, shared agency, divine abundance, and messianic identity meet in one meal.

questions.question: Why must the Messiah suffer?
questions.answer: Dei, ‘must,’ marks the path as belonging to God's scriptural purpose, not as an accident after Peter's confession. Elders, chief priests, scribes, and executioners still act responsibly; divine necessity does not make human violence good. Resurrection belongs to the same sentence as rejection and death.

questions.question: Why does the hosted English omit Luke's distinctive ‘daily’ in 9:23?
questions.answer: The locally hosted SBL Greek includes kath’ hēmeran, ‘day by day,’ a strongly attested Lukan addition to the cross saying, while the WEB line here follows a form without it. The variant matters because Luke often turns future expectation into daily discipleship. Readers can see the Greek word layer even when this English edition omits it.

questions.question: What are Moses and Elijah discussing with Jesus?
questions.answer: Luke calls it his exodos, ‘departure,’ which he is about to fulfill in Jerusalem. The word can include death, resurrection, and ascension while recalling Israel's exodus. Moses and Elijah do not merely pose for a vision; Scripture's law and prophets interpret the road ahead.

questions.question: Why rebuke the disciples for wanting Elijah-like fire?
questions.answer: A Samaritan village refuses lodging because Jesus is headed to Jerusalem, reflecting real Judean-Samaritan conflict. James and John turn scriptural precedent into retaliatory violence; Jesus turns and rebukes them. The journey rejects holy-war vengeance and will soon make a Samaritan the example of neighbor-love.

questions.question: Do the final call sayings forbid funerals and family goodbyes?
questions.answer: The sayings use prophetic urgency and deliberate shock to expose delay, divided priority, and nostalgia. ‘Let the dead bury their dead’ contrasts kingdom proclamation with socially unquestioned obligation; the plow image demands forward attention. They should not be weaponized to evade care or control converts through isolation.

glossary.def: God's anointed king; Luke immediately joins the title to rejection, death, and resurrection.
Roman instrument of execution and public shame, not originally a generic word for inconvenience.
Departure or way out; Luke's word for what Jesus will fulfill at Jerusalem.
Scriptural idiom for resolute purpose and chosen direction.
